reading.body:
Equinix SV8 in Palo Alto is a 26,296 square foot colocation facility with N+1 redundancy across power, cooling, and generators, but its actual power capacity in megawatts remains unpublished.

The lack of published MW figures for individual facilities obscures how much compute capacity Equinix can actually serve in Silicon Valley. SV8 is one of twelve facilities in the region that collectively claim to serve over 10,500 customers, yet the power envelope for each building is invisible to outside analysis. This matters because AI workloads are power-constrained, and colocation pricing and availability depend on whether a facility has spare power to allocate. Without capacity figures, one cannot assess whether Silicon Valley's largest retail colocation footprint has headroom for additional AI compute or is already power-limited.

N+1 redundancy means the facility can tolerate one simultaneous failure in any of three critical systems without service loss. This is standard practice for enterprise colocation but does not indicate whether the facility is designed for the continuous, intensive power draw of modern AI training or inference clusters. The redundancy tier and square footage tell you the facility exists and meets baseline availability requirements. They do not tell you its thermal design, power density per rack, or whether its cooling systems can handle the heat signatures of GPUs and custom accelerators that now dominate customer demand.
